# Welcome! {.unnumbered} This is a **Personal Finance field manual**: a working reference for the day-to-day decisions that shape your financial life. It covers budgeting, saving, borrowing, investing, taxes, insurance, and planning. :::: {.callout-tip collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Who this book is for]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} The primary audience for this book is my children. It contains some of the basic principles I was taught (and others I've learned painfully) about managing personal finances. ::: :::: This book aims to answer questions like: * "*Where is my money going each month?*" * "*How much should I have in an emergency fund?*" * "*Should I pay down debt or invest first?*" * "*Which retirement account makes sense for me?*" * "*How do I pick an index fund?*" :::: {.callout-important collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Who wrote this?]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} Given the current landscape of online resources and the impressive capabilities of AI/large language models (LLMs), I feel it’s important to clarify the authorship of this book. It seems strange to have to include this in anything I write, but it’s something that, if I were reading a book, I’d like to know. [I wrote all of the narrative, commentary, and explanations.]{style='color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;'} I used LLMs (mostly Claude) to research specific topics (like FDIC/NCUA coverage), but the thoughts in the book are my own. Hopefully, the typos and/or grammatical errors serve as a signature of authenticity. [The code in this book was created with the assistance of Claude, and this applies only to the specific chapters explicitly noted.]{style='color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;'} Generally, I’d write a ‘first draft’ of a code example, then ask Claude how to improve it. Sometimes I agreed with its suggestions (and included them), other times I revised the code myself. ::: :::: ## How this book is organized The book is divided into five parts: 1. [**Foundations**](foundations.qmd): income, tracking spending, budgeting, debt, and emergency funds. 2. [**Savings**](savings.qmd): savings strategies, high-yield accounts, and automation. 3. [**Investing**](investing.qmd): the basics, retirement accounts, index funds, and asset allocation. 4. [**Taxes & insurance**](taxes_insurance.qmd): the protective layer around your finances. 5. [**Planning**](planning.qmd): goals, major purchases, and estate planning. The five sections of the book map into [four levers]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}: ## The four levers | Lever | Question | |-----------|---------------------------| | Income | How much comes in? | | Spending | How much goes out? | | Savings | How much is set aside? | | Investing | What happens to the rest? | The diagram shows how the levers connect, and which part of the book covers each one. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'The Four Levers' %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false, "fontSize":"16px"}}}%% flowchart LR subgraph Foundations["Foundations"] Income("Income
How much comes in?") Spending("Spending
How much goes out?") end subgraph SavingsPart["Savings"] Savings("Savings
How much is set aside?") end subgraph InvestingPart["Investing"] Investing("Investing
What happens to the rest?") end Income --> Spending Spending --> Savings Savings --> Investing style Income fill:#48a56a,color:#F5F2E8,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style Spending fill:#0e9aa7,color:#F5F2E8,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style Savings fill:#0e9aa7,color:#F5F2E8,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style Investing fill:#48a56a,color:#F5F2E8,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style Foundations fill:#FFFFFF,color:#1C1C1E,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style SavingsPart fill:#FFFFFF,color:#1C1C1E,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px style InvestingPart fill:#FFFFFF,color:#1C1C1E,stroke:#1C1C1E,stroke-width:2px ``` Each lever has its own part in this book: * [Foundations](foundations.qmd): [Income]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}, [budgeting]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}, and [spending]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"} are the behaviors that will have the biggest impact on your financial health. You'll also want to manage the money you borrow, and plan for emergencies. * [Savings](savings.qmd) covers different ways to put money aside, different kinds of savings accounts, and the most important behavior for disciplined savings: [automation]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}.\ * [Investing](investing.qmd) is what happens to the money you save [over the long term]{style="color:#48a56a; font-weight: bold;"}. * [Taxes & insurance](taxes_insurance.qmd) & [Planning](planning.qmd) sit around the outside. Each chapter is short and self-contained so you can jump in where you need to. ## Math Whatever math is covered in this book can be done with a calculator, spreadsheet, or some basic programming skills. If you're interested in following along or performing any of the calculations yourself, I've provided examples in Microsoft Excel and both **R** and **Python**. Example R code: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} 1000 * (1 + 0.05)^10 # future value of $1,000 at 5% for 10 years #> [1] 1628.895 ``` ::: Example Python code: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} 1000 * (1 + 0.05) ** 10 #> 1628.894626777442 ``` ::: If you're interested in programming, the book also has an [accompanying website](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/dev-fm-finance/) where I dive a little deeper into R/Python functions, package development, and how to create interactive web applications using the Shiny framework. ## About the author Martin Frigaard writes about R packages, Shiny applications, and, now, personal finance.
